## Why This Matters

The coqui detector from L02 works — and the field team is unhappy with it anyway.
Their kNN labels every recording with the same flat certainty, but the biologists'
workflow runs on *confidence*: a detection they can trust gets filed automatically; a
borderline one gets a human listen. "Which calls should we double-check?" is a
question a bare label cannot answer.

This lesson upgrades the detector's output from a label to a **probability** — and on
the way, settles what classification problems look like and how a linear model can
solve them.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
A label is a verdict; a probability is a verdict **with the jury's vote count
attached**. "Guilty, 7 votes to 5" and "guilty, 12 to 0" lead to very different
appeals — and "portoricensis, p = 0.52" earns a human review that "p = 0.97" does not.
:::

## The Classification Problem

Regression (L03) predicts a quantity. Classification predicts a **category** — and
the structure of the output sorts the problems into three variants:

| Variant | The output is... | Fresh example |
|---------|------------------|---------------|
| **Binary** | one of exactly two classes | will this loan default — yes or no? |
| **Multiclass** | one of three or more classes | which fault caused this power outage — vegetation, equipment, weather, or demand? |
| **Multilabel** | *several* classes at once may apply | which topics does this news article touch — politics, economy, sports...? |

This lesson teaches binary classification first and extends it to multiclass at the
end; multilabel is defined here so the term is not a stranger, and not taught.

## Why Not Just Fit a Line?

We own a working tool for numbers — so encode the classes as numbers ($y = 0$ for
*coqui*, $y = 1$ for *portoricensis*), fit linear regression, done? Almost — and the
"almost" is instructive. A line happily outputs $1.4$ or $-0.3$: what probability is
140%? Worse, the line's predictions drift with the data's geometry — add a few very
high-pitched calls and the fitted line tilts, dragging the place where it crosses 0.5
even though those far-away calls were never in doubt.

What we want keeps the linear machinery — a weighted sum of features, learned from
data — but pins the output into $(0, 1)$ so it can honestly be a probability.

## The Sigmoid: A Squash for Scores

Logistic regression computes the same linear score as L03 and then squashes it:

$$\hat{p} = \sigma(t), \qquad t = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + \dots + b_p x_p, \qquad \sigma(t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-t}}$$

The **sigmoid** $\sigma$ is an S-shaped curve with exactly the properties needed:

| Score $t$ | $\sigma(t)$ | Reading |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| very negative | near 0 | confidently the negative class |
| $0$ | exactly $0.5$ | the model's coin flip |
| very positive | near 1 | confidently the positive class |

No score, however extreme, escapes $(0, 1)$ — the squash is what makes "the model is
83% sure" a meaningful sentence. The full pipeline from measurement to label:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  X["Features x<br/>(co, qui pitch)"] --> S["Linear score<br/>t = b0 + b1 x1 + b2 x2"]
  S --> G["Sigmoid<br/>p = 1/(1+e^-t)"]
  G --> T{"p >= 0.5 ?"}
  T -->|yes| P["portoricensis"]
  T -->|no| C["coqui"]
```

Everything before the threshold is smooth and probabilistic; the threshold is the
last, deliberately blunt step — and the lab shows why you sometimes move it.

## Decision Boundaries

Where does the model switch answers? Exactly where $\hat{p} = 0.5$, which by the
table above means **where the linear score $t = 0$** — and "$b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2
= 0$" is the equation of a straight line in the feature plane. That line is the
**decision boundary**: calls on one side get one label, calls on the other side get
the other, and calls *near* it are precisely the ones with probabilities near 0.5.

This is what "logistic regression is a **linear classifier**" means: whatever the
probabilities do, the label-switching frontier is a line (a flat plane with more
features). When the true frontier between classes is genuinely curved, a linear
classifier caps out early — that limitation is real, and later tools (Unit IV trees,
Unit V networks) exist largely to lift it.

## Training: The Log Loss

What loss should training minimize? MSE belongs to regression; for probabilities the
natural currency is surprise. The **log loss** charges the model the negative log of
the probability it assigned to the *true* class:

| True class | Model said | Loss $-\log(\hat{p}_{\text{true}})$ | Verdict |
|------------|-----------|--------------------------------------|---------|
| portoricensis | $\hat{p} = 0.9$ | $0.11$ | cheap — confident and right |
| portoricensis | $\hat{p} = 0.5$ | $0.69$ | mediocre — hedging |
| portoricensis | $\hat{p} = 0.1$ | $2.30$ | expensive — confident and wrong |

Averaged over the training set:

$$L = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \Big[ y_i \log \hat{p}_i + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - \hat{p}_i) \Big]$$

The bracket picks the term that matches each example's true label; the cost explodes
as the model gets *confidently* wrong, which is exactly the behavior to punish in a
probability machine. Unlike least squares, this loss has **no closed-form minimizer**
— there is no normal equation to jump to. But it is convex (one bowl, one bottom), so
**gradient descent** — the general route L03 named — reliably finds the best
coefficients. This is why that name mattered.

## Softmax: Three or More Classes

For $K$ classes, give each class its own linear score $s_k(x)$, then convert the
score vector into probabilities with the **softmax**: exponentiate every score and
normalize,

$$\hat{p}_k = \frac{e^{s_k(x)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{s_j(x)}}$$

The outputs are positive and sum to 1 — one probability per class — and the model
predicts the class with the largest (the *argmax*). Binary logistic regression is the $K = 2$
special case (one score pinned to zero recovers the sigmoid). scikit-learn's
`LogisticRegression` switches to softmax automatically when it sees more than two
classes; the lab runs it on the three iris species.

## When to Use / When NOT to Use

- **Use it when:** you need probabilities, not just labels; you want a strong,
  fast, interpretable baseline (one readable weight per feature); the classes are
  roughly separable by a line/plane.
- **Avoid it when:** the boundary is clearly nonlinear (a linear classifier caps
  out); you need the model to *describe* each class rather than just separate them
  (that is the generative view — Gaussian discriminant analysis and Naive Bayes,
  L06-L07).

## Common Pitfalls

- **Treating 0.5 as sacred.** It is the default threshold, not a law. When classes
  are imbalanced (1 fraud in 1,000 transactions) or mistakes cost differently, the
  right threshold moves — the lab's Exercise 1 does this deliberately.
- **Reading accuracy as the whole story.** A 0.853 hides *which* calls fail and how
  confidently. Unit III builds the proper instruments (confusion-based metrics);
  this lesson plants the probability-level habit.
- **Reading probabilities as guarantees.** $\hat{p} = 0.73$ means "given what I
  learned, calls like this are portoricensis about 73% of the time" — the lab finds
  a 73%-confident mistake. Estimates, not promises.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: the logit, or why 'regression' (Optional)" collapse="true"}

Invert the sigmoid and you find what the linear score *is*:

$$t = \log \frac{\hat{p}}{1 - \hat{p}}$$

— the log of the odds, called the **logit**. So logistic regression is ordinary
linear regression *on the log-odds scale*: the model is linear in $t$, and each
coefficient $b_j$ is the change in log-odds per unit of feature $j$ (equivalently,
multiplying the odds by $e^{b_j}$). That is the historical name's logic — it
regresses the logit — and it is why the fitted coefficients remain readable: sign
says which class the feature pushes toward, magnitude says how hard, in odds.
:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Why is it called *regression* if it classifies?"** — Because under the hood it
*is* a regression — on the log-odds scale (see the Deep Dive). The name confuses
everyone once; in practice, remember: target a quantity, linear regression; target a
class, logistic regression.

**"Can I trust the probabilities?"** — Mostly, for logistic regression — its training
objective directly rewards honest probabilities, and it is among the better-calibrated
models out of the box. But calibration degrades when the training data is small,
imbalanced, or unlike deployment data. Professionals check calibration before
treating 0.9 as 90% (a Unit III concern); until then, trust the *ordering* (0.9 is
more credible than 0.6) more than the exact values.

**"For 10 classes, do I train 10 binary models?"** — You can — that strategy is
called one-vs-rest, and it works. But softmax handles all classes in one model with
probabilities that sum to 1 by construction, and it is the default in scikit-learn.
You will meet the same softmax again as the final layer of every classification
neural network in Unit V.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Classification | predict a category; binary / multiclass / multilabel by output |
| Logistic regression | linear score, squashed by the sigmoid into a probability |
| Sigmoid | maps any score to (0,1); score 0 lands on 0.5 |
| Decision boundary | where the label switches; linear here (score = 0) |
| Threshold | the dial that turns probability into label; 0.5 is a default, not a law |
| Log loss | pay -log(p of the true class); confident errors cost the most |
| Softmax | one score per class, exponentiate and normalize; predict the argmax |
| predict_proba | the lab's workhorse — probabilities, not just labels |
